code.title: SIGTERM can be caught, SIGKILL cannot
code.python:
import os, signal, subprocess, sys, time

# SIGTERM can be caught: the handler runs and the process exits cleanly.
def on_term(signum, frame):
    print("child: got SIGTERM, flushing and exiting cleanly")
    sys.stdout.flush()
    os._exit(0)

if len(sys.argv) > 1:               # child mode
    signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, on_term)
    print("child: ready", flush=True)
    time.sleep(30)
    sys.exit(1)

# SIGKILL cannot be caught: the kernel refuses to install a handler.
try:
    signal.signal(signal.SIGKILL, lambda s, f: None)
except OSError as e:
    print("parent: cannot catch SIGKILL ->", e.strerror)

p = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, __file__, "child"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
print(p.stdout.readline().strip())
p.send_signal(signal.SIGTERM)       # polite request first
print(p.stdout.read().strip())
print("exit code after SIGTERM:", p.wait())

q = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(30)"])
time.sleep(0.3)
q.kill()                            # SIGKILL: no cleanup runs
print("exit code after SIGKILL:", q.wait(), "(negative = killed by signal 9, shell shows 137)")

followUps:
Shells report a process killed by a signal as 128 plus the signal number, and SIGTERM is signal 15, so 128 + 15 = 143.

The same rule gives 130 for Ctrl-C (SIGINT, 2) and 137 for SIGKILL (9). A process that catches SIGTERM and calls exit(0) reports 0 instead, so 143 means it died from the default action or a handler re-raised it. Python and other wait APIs show a negative value, such as -15, for the same event.

It is usually stuck in uninterruptible sleep (state D), waiting inside the kernel for something like a dead NFS server or a failing disk.

Signals are only delivered when the task leaves the kernel, so SIGKILL stays pending. Check with ps -o stat,wchan -p PID. A zombie (state Z) also ignores kill because it is already dead and only waits for its parent to reap it. The fix is to restore the device or mount, or reboot as a last resort.

Kubernetes first runs the preStop hook, and SIGTERM is sent to the container's main process only after the hook finishes (or concurrently on some versions, so do not rely on ordering).

The grace period (default 30 s, terminationGracePeriodSeconds) starts when the pod is marked Terminating and covers both preStop and shutdown. If the process is still alive when it runs out, the kubelet sends SIGKILL. Example: preStop sleeps 10 s, the app needs 15 s, so 25 s fits in 30 s. The pod is also removed from service endpoints at that moment, which is why a short preStop sleep helps drain traffic.

code.title: Decode octal modes into rwx

followUps:
umask is a mask of permission bits that are removed from the mode of every new file or directory a process creates.

New files start at 666 and directories at 777, then the umask bits are cleared. With the common umask 022: file 666 - 022 = 644 and directory 777 - 022 = 755. With umask 077 files become 600 and directories 700, which is private to the owner. It is inherited from the parent shell and set with umask 027. It only affects creation, never existing files.

It is enforced by the SSH client itself, not the kernel: OpenSSH refuses to use a private key that other users can read.

It checks the key file mode and prints "UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE" if group or others have any access. With 600 (rw-------) only the owner can read it, so other local users cannot copy it. The kernel then enforces the 600 bits on every open(). Also keep ~/.ssh at 700, and the server's StrictModes applies similar checks to authorized_keys.

With r but no x you can list the names in the directory, but you cannot access anything inside it by name.

For example ls dir shows file names, but ls -l dir and cat dir/file fail with "Permission denied" because reading an inode or entering the path needs x. The reverse, x without r, lets you open a file if you already know its exact name, but not list the directory. That second form is used for "drop boxes" and hidden paths.

code.title: Redirection order with dup2: > out 2>&1
code.python:
import os, subprocess, tempfile

# Child writes "OUT" to fd 1 and "ERR" to fd 2. We apply redirections in two orders.
child = "import os; os.write(1, b'OUT\\n'); os.write(2, b'ERR\\n')"
d = tempfile.mkdtemp()

def run(order):
    path = os.path.join(d, order + ".txt")
    f = os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC)
    read_err, write_err = os.pipe()   # stands in for the terminal
    def setup():
        if order == "out_then_err":    # cmd > out 2>&1
            os.dup2(f, 1)              # fd1 -> file
            os.dup2(1, 2)              # fd2 copies fd1 (the file)
        else:                          # cmd 2>&1 > out
            os.dup2(write_err, 2)      # fd2 copies "terminal" (fd1 old target)
            os.dup2(f, 1)              # then fd1 -> file
    p = subprocess.Popen(["python3", "-c", child], preexec_fn=setup, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
    p.wait()
    os.close(write_err)
    on_terminal = os.read(read_err, 100)
    print(order, "-> file:", open(path).read().split(), "| terminal:", on_terminal.decode().split())

run("out_then_err")   # both lines land in the file
run("err_then_out")   # only OUT lands in the file; ERR went to the "terminal"

followUps:
Redirect stderr into the pipe and stdout away: cmd 2>&1 >/dev/null | grep ERR.

Order matters. First fd 2 copies fd 1, which still points at the pipe. Then fd 1 is sent to /dev/null. The result is that only stderr reaches grep. In bash you can also write cmd 2> >(grep ERR) with process substitution, which keeps stdout on the terminal. Bash 4+ has |& for sending both streams into the pipe.

Because stdout is usually buffered and stderr is not, so stderr bytes are written the moment they happen while stdout waits for the buffer to fill or flush.

When stdout goes to a file the C library uses full buffering (for example 4096 bytes), whereas on a terminal it is line buffered. A program printing "start" to stdout and then an error to stderr will put the error first in the file. Fix it with stdbuf -oL cmd, flushing in the program, or fflush(stdout).

dup2(old, new) makes descriptor new point to the same open file as old, closing new first if needed. It is the system call behind every redirection.

The shell forks, then in the child runs dup2(fd_of_out, 1) for > out and dup2(1, 2) for 2>&1 before calling exec. The new program inherits those descriptors and has no idea it was redirected. The order of dup2 calls is exactly the left-to-right order of the redirections.

code.title: Top client IPs: the pipeline stage by stage
code.python:
from collections import Counter

# Same result as: awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -3
log = """10.0.0.1 - GET /a 200
10.0.0.2 - GET /b 500
10.0.0.1 - GET /c 200
10.0.0.3 - GET /a 200
10.0.0.1 - GET /d 500
10.0.0.2 - GET /a 200""".splitlines()

# Stage 1 (awk): take the first field of each line
ips = [line.split()[0] for line in log]
print("stage1:", ips)

# Stage 2+3 (sort | uniq -c): sorting groups equal IPs so uniq can count neighbours
counts = []
for ip in sorted(ips):
    if counts and counts[-1][0] == ip:
        counts[-1][1] += 1
    else:
        counts.append([ip, 1])
print("stage3:", counts)

# Stage 4+5 (sort -nr | head): biggest counts first, keep the top N
top = sorted(counts, key=lambda c: -c[1])[:3]
print("top:", top)

# The O(n) shortcut: a hash map counts without sorting (like an awk array)
print("hash :", Counter(ips).most_common(3))

followUps:
Filter with awk before counting: awk '$9 == 500 {print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10.

In the common combined log format the status code is field 9, so the test keeps only 500 lines before the IP is extracted. Check your own format first, because a different field layout shifts the number. Filtering early also shrinks the data the sorts have to handle, which helps time and memory. The cost is still O(n) for the scan plus O(m log m) for sorting m matching lines.

Decompress to a stream and feed it into the same pipeline: zcat access.log*.gz | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10.

Use zcat -f (or zgrep) to mix plain and gzipped files, since rotated logs often have both. Nothing is written to disk, so memory stays flat while gunzip runs at hundreds of MB/s. For bzip2 or xz use bzcat or xzcat. Include the live log in the glob so you do not miss the newest requests.

Avoid a full sort and keep the work parallel and bounded: count with a hash table, shard the data, then merge.

1) Use awk '{c[$1]++} END{for(i in c) print c[i],i}', which needs memory only for distinct IPs (millions of IPs is fine). 2) If that is too big, split the file by hash of the IP into 16 pieces, count each, and merge. 3) GNU sort already spills to temp files, so set -S 2G -T /big/tmp --parallel=8. 4) Or load it into a columnar tool such as DuckDB. Time is O(n) with counting, O(n log n) with sorting.

code.title: Graceful shutdown with a signal flag
code.python:
import os, signal, time

# Handler only sets a flag; the main loop does the real cleanup (safe pattern).
stop = {"requested": False, "signal": None}

def handler(signum, frame):
    stop["requested"] = True
    stop["signal"] = signal.Signals(signum).name

signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, handler)
signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, handler)

queue = ["job1", "job2", "job3", "job4", "job5"]
in_flight = []
done = []
tick = 0
while queue or in_flight:
    tick += 1
    if tick == 3:
        os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGTERM)   # simulate the orchestrator
        time.sleep(0.05)
    if stop["requested"] and queue:
        print("tick", tick, "got", stop["signal"], "- stop accepting, dropping", queue)
        queue.clear()                          # stop taking new work
    if queue:
        in_flight.append(queue.pop(0))
    if in_flight:
        done.append(in_flight.pop(0))          # drain in-flight work
        print("tick", tick, "finished", done[-1])
print("flushing, closing, exit 0 with done =", done)

followUps:
Because the C library's printf takes locks and allocates memory, and a signal can interrupt the program in the middle of that same code.

If the main thread is inside malloc or printf holding its lock and the handler calls printf, the handler waits for a lock the interrupted code owns: a deadlock, or corrupted buffers. Only async-signal-safe functions such as write, _exit and sigaction are allowed. Safest practice is to set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, or write(2, msg, len) a short message.

The signal can arrive between the flag check and the call to pause(), so pause() then sleeps forever and the shutdown is missed.

Sequence: the loop tests !flag (true), the handler runs and sets flag = 1, then pause() starts and nothing else will wake it. The cure is to block the signal with sigprocmask and use sigsuspend or ppoll/pselect, which atomically unblock and wait. A self-pipe or signalfd avoids the problem entirely.

PID 1 gets special treatment: the kernel does not apply default signal actions to it, so a SIGTERM with no handler is simply ignored and the container waits for SIGKILL.

Your service must install a SIGTERM handler explicitly, or you run a small init such as tini with docker run --init, which forwards signals and reaps zombie children. Also use the exec form CMD ["app"] in the Dockerfile, because the shell form puts sh at PID 1 and it does not forward SIGTERM to your app.

code.title: A zombie appears until the parent reaps it

followUps:
An orphan is a child that is still running after its parent has died, while a zombie is a child that has already finished but not been reaped.

The orphan keeps running and is adopted by PID 1 (or the nearest subreaper), which later reaps it normally, so orphans are harmless. A zombie shows state Z in ps and uses only a process-table slot. Example: a parent exits while its child sleeps 100 s (orphan). A parent that loops forever and never waits on a child that exited creates a zombie.

Because Linux merges several SIGCHLD signals into one if they arrive while the handler is pending, so one signal can mean many dead children.

If three children exit together, the handler may run once. A single waitpid would reap one child and leave two zombies. Looping while (waitpid(-1, &st, WNOHANG) > 0) reaps everything that is ready and stops as soon as none is left, without blocking. Save and restore errno inside the handler.

Run ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,cmd | awk '$3 ~ /^Z/', since zombies have a state starting with Z and show as <defunct>.

The PPID column tells you whose fault it is, because that parent must reap them. Count them with ps -eo stat | grep -c '^Z'. top also shows "N zombie" in its header. Example output: 4121 3990 Z [worker] <defunct>. Then investigate or restart process 3990.

The kernel ignores setuid on scripts because there is a race between checking the script and the interpreter opening it, which attackers can exploit.

When you run #!/bin/sh script, the kernel starts the interpreter with the script path as an argument. An attacker could swap the file (or use a symlink) between the permission check and the interpreter opening it, so a root shell runs attacker-chosen code. Scripts also inherit risky things like IFS and PATH. Use a compiled wrapper, sudo with a fixed command, or capabilities instead.

Capabilities split root's all-powerful authority into about 40 separate rights, so a program can get only the one it needs.

Examples: CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE allows binding ports below 1024, CAP_SYS_TIME sets the clock, CAP_KILL bypasses signal permission checks. A web server can run as a normal user with setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /usr/bin/app and listen on port 80, and a compromise cannot read other users' files. Inspect them with getcap -r /usr/bin or capsh --print.

List every file with the setuid or setgid bit, compare it with a known-good baseline, and alert on changes.

Command: find / -xdev \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -type f -ls 2>/dev/null. Save the output after install, then diff it daily (or let AIDE/auditd watch it). Check each hit: does it need the bit, is the package owner trusted, is it writable only by root? Remove with chmod u-s file and mount user-writable filesystems with nosuid.

It is the percentage of time the virtual machine's CPU was ready to run but the hypervisor gave the physical CPU to another guest.

If steal is 20%, a fifth of your CPU time is lost to noisy neighbours or an oversubscribed host, so the app feels slow even though your own processes look idle. It shows as st in top and vmstat. The fix is a bigger or dedicated instance, or moving to a less busy host. It does not exist on bare metal.

Because a process waiting on a hard-mounted NFS server is in uninterruptible sleep, and the kernel will not interrupt it until the server answers.

Hard mounts retry forever to protect data, so a dead server leaves every process touching the mount in state D, and even kill -9 stays pending. Soft mounts return an I/O error after a timeout but can corrupt data. The intr option is obsolete, though modern kernels do allow fatal signals on NFS waits. Best cure is to restore the server, or use umount -f or -l.

PSI (pressure stall information) is a kernel metric showing how much time tasks spent stalled waiting for CPU, memory or I/O.

Read /proc/pressure/io: some avg10=12.50 avg60=8.00 avg300=3.00 total=... means that in the last 10 seconds, at least one task was stalled on I/O for 12.5% of the time. The full line means all tasks were stalled. It is more direct than load average because it separates cause (cpu, memory, io) and gives percentages. cgroup v2 has per-group files too.

SO_REUSEPORT lets several sockets in different processes bind to the same address and port, and the kernel spreads incoming connections among them.

Without it, a second bind returns "Address already in use". With it, each of 4 worker processes can listen on :8080 and the kernel hashes each new connection to one listener, giving load balancing without a shared accept lock. All sockets must set the option and run as the same user. It differs from SO_REUSEADDR, which mostly allows binding while old connections are in TIME_WAIT.

A real listener has state LISTEN, whereas TIME_WAIT is a closed connection that the kernel keeps for about 60 seconds, and it has no owning process.

Use ss -ltn 'sport = :8080' to see only LISTEN sockets. ss -tan state time-wait lists the others, and -p shows no process for them. TIME_WAIT on a port does not stop a new server from binding if it sets SO_REUSEADDR, which most servers do. Many TIME_WAIT entries are normal for busy clients.

Find the pod, then look inside its network namespace, since the port belongs to the pod and not to the node.

Run kubectl get pods -A -o wide and kubectl get svc -A | grep 8080 to match the service and pod. Then kubectl exec POD -- ss -ltnp (or kubectl debug with an ephemeral container if the image has no ss). For hostPort or hostNetwork pods, run ss on the node itself. kubectl port-forward also uses local ports, so check there if the clash is on your laptop.

code.title: Reading live kernel state from /proc
code.python:
import os

# /proc files are generated by the kernel when read; nothing is stored on disk.
with open("/proc/self/status") as f:
    fields = dict(line.split(":", 1) for line in f if ":" in line)
print("Name    =", fields["Name"].strip())
print("State   =", fields["State"].strip().split()[0], "(R = running, this process is reading)")
print("Threads =", fields["Threads"].strip())

# /proc/PID/fd is a directory of symlinks, which is how lsof lists open files
target = os.path.realpath("/proc/self/exe")
print("exe is a python binary:", "python" in os.path.basename(target))
print("fd 0,1,2 exist:", all(os.path.exists("/proc/self/fd/%d" % i) for i in (0, 1, 2)))

# cmdline is NUL-separated argv; ps reads exactly this
argv = open("/proc/self/cmdline").read().split("\0")[:-1]
print("argv items:", len(argv))

# `uptime` just parses this file: three load averages, runnable/total, last pid
print("loadavg has 5 fields:", len(open("/proc/loadavg").read().split()) == 5)
print("pid matches:", os.readlink("/proc/self") == str(os.getpid()))

followUps:
VSZ is all virtual address space a process has mapped, RSS is the part currently in RAM, and PSS is RSS with shared pages divided fairly among the processes sharing them.

Example: two processes each map a 10 MB shared library fully in RAM. Each has RSS 10 MB from the library, so summing RSS counts 20 MB, but PSS gives 5 MB each and sums to the true 10 MB. VSZ can be huge (many GB) because it includes reserved but unused memory. Read PSS from /proc/PID/smaps_rollup.

Because many programs receive passwords, API keys and tokens through environment variables, and /proc/PID/environ shows them as plain text.

It is readable by the process owner and root, and ps eww shows them too. Any bug that lets an attacker read files as that user, or a debug dump, leaks the secrets, and child processes inherit them. Prefer secret files with mode 600, or a secrets manager, unset variables after reading them, and avoid putting secrets on the command line, which appears in cmdline.

/proc describes processes and the running kernel, while /sys (sysfs) exposes the kernel's device and driver model as a structured tree of one-value files.

In /proc you find /proc/PID/status, meminfo, cpuinfo and tunables in /proc/sys. In /sys you find hardware: /sys/class/net/eth0/speed, /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler, CPU frequency and the cgroup tree. The rule in /sys is one value per file, whereas /proc files are free-form text that tools must parse.

A futex wait means the thread is sleeping because it wants a lock, condition variable or similar user-space synchronisation primitive that another thread holds.

In strace you see futex(0x7f..., FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE, ...) with no return. If many threads show this, you have lock contention or a deadlock, and the cure is to find the lock holder, for example with gdb -p PID -batch -ex 'thread apply all bt'. An uncontended lock never enters the kernel, so seeing futex calls at all signals contention.

Filter by syscall name with -e: strace -f -e trace=openat -p PID, or -e trace=file for all file-related calls.

Use -f to follow threads and child processes, and -o out.txt to write to a file so the program's output is not mixed in. A line like openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/app.conf", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT instantly shows a missing config file. For lower cost in production use perf trace -e openat or bpftrace's opensnoop.

ltrace traces calls to shared library functions (such as malloc, strlen, printf) instead of kernel system calls.

For example ltrace -c ./app counts how often each libc function is called, and ltrace -e malloc+free ./app shows allocations and frees. It works by patching the program's PLT entries, so it only sees dynamically linked calls, not statically linked code or inlined functions. It is slow and less used than strace today, and it fails on some modern binaries (PIE, hardened builds). For deeper tracing use uprobes via perf or bpftrace.

Type=simple treats the process as started the moment it is forked, forking waits for the parent to exit and uses the child as the main PID, notify waits for the app to send READY=1, and oneshot waits for the process to finish.

Use simple for most modern services, notify when other units must wait until the service is really ready (a database that has loaded), forking only for old daemons that double-fork (give PIDFile=), and oneshot for scripts such as migrations, often with RemainAfterExit=yes.

Wants and Requires say what to start together, and After says what order; they are independent, and you usually need both.

Wants=b.service starts b but tolerates its failure. Requires=b.service fails or stops this unit if b fails. Neither orders anything: without After=b.service both start in parallel. Example: a web app with Requires=db.service and After=db.service starts after the database and stops with it. BindsTo is a stricter form of Requires.

Socket activation lets systemd own the listening socket, so connections queue in the kernel while the service starts or restarts, and nothing is refused.

With a .socket unit systemd binds port 80, and when the first connection arrives it starts the service and passes the open socket as file descriptor 3 (via LISTEN_FDS). On restart, the socket stays open, so clients wait in the backlog for a moment rather than seeing "connection refused". It also allows lazy start and starting services in parallel at boot.

oom_score_adj shifts how likely the OOM killer is to pick a process; the range is -1000 to +1000, and a higher value makes the process more likely to die.

The kernel's badness score is roughly the share of memory the process uses plus the adjustment. Setting -1000 makes a process immune (used for sshd), and +500 volunteers a batch job as the first victim. Check it with cat /proc/PID/oom_score_adj and /proc/PID/oom_score. Kubernetes sets it from the QoS class: Guaranteed pods get -997, BestEffort 1000.

A cgroup OOM kill happens when a group reaches its own memory limit, even though the host has plenty of free memory, while a host OOM happens when the entire machine runs out.

The cgroup kill picks a victim only inside that group, and is logged as "Memory cgroup out of memory" with the oom_kill counter in memory.events going up. A host OOM scans every process on the machine and may hit an unrelated service. The first is fixed by raising the limit or the app's memory use, the second by capacity, swap or evicting neighbours.

Alert on memory pressure and approaching limits, not just on the kill that follows.

Watch working-set memory divided by limit (for example warn at 85%), the PSI memory some value, and swap or page-fault rate. Also alert on any increase of the oom_kill counter in memory.events (or node_vmstat_oom_kill in Prometheus) and on container restarts with reason OOMKilled. A steady upward trend over hours suggests a leak, so capture a heap profile early.

flock takes an advisory lock on a file, and a second run that tries the same lock either waits or fails at once, so only one copy runs.

Use flock -n /var/lock/cleanup.lock ./cleanup.sh: with -n a second instance exits immediately with status 1. The lock is tied to the open file and the kernel drops it when the process dies, so there are no stale lock files (unlike a hand-made pid file). It is advisory, so every script must use the same lock file, and it does not work reliably across NFS.

If DIR is empty, "$DIR/" becomes /, and rm -rf then tries to delete the whole filesystem.

Example: DIR=$(cat missing.conf); rm -rf "$DIR/" expands to rm -rf /. GNU rm refuses "/" by default (--preserve-root), but rm -rf /* or /home/ patterns are not protected. Guard with ${DIR:?not set}, which aborts when the variable is unset or empty, and check that the path starts with an expected prefix.

Write the exact list of files before deleting them, log the deletions with a timestamp, and send both to central storage.

Run find ... -print0 > /var/log/cleanup/list-$(date +%F).lst, then delete from that same list with xargs -0 rm -v so the log matches reality. Ship the journal to a central log system, record total count and bytes, and alert if the count is far above normal. For irreversible data, move files to a quarantine folder for 7 days before real deletion, or use filesystem snapshots.

A good sandbox profile gives the agent only what the task needs: a container or VM, an unprivileged user, a small writable workspace, and no more network than required.

Contents: read-only root filesystem and source mount; a writable /workspace only; --cap-drop=ALL and no-new-privileges; a seccomp profile; cgroup limits such as 2 GB memory, 100 PIDs and 1 CPU; egress allow-list to the package mirror and git host; no secrets in the environment; a wall-clock timeout that ends the sandbox.

You cannot reliably stop injection with prompts alone, so you limit what the shell can do even when the model is tricked.

Treat text from files, web pages and tool results as untrusted data. Layers: allow-list commands (or require human approval for deletion, network, and anything outside the workspace), run in a sandbox with no secrets and restricted egress so a successful injection cannot exfiltrate anything, and parse and validate arguments rather than passing model text to sh -c. Review the plan before execution for risky actions.

Record every command and its result in a tamper-resistant log, and make each session reproducible and attributable.

Log the timestamp, user or agent identity, working directory, full command line, exit code, and a hash of key files, sent to a separate append-only store the agent cannot edit (auditd execve rules, shell session recording, or the sandbox's own audit trail). Keep git diffs of the workspace. Afterwards, search for risky patterns such as rm -rf, curl | sh or reads of ~/.ssh, and compare the file changes with the stated task.
